00---index--and--project-overview.title: 00 - Index & Project Overview
00---index--and--project-overview.content:
Serverless Workflow & Data Passing Models in faas-sim
Project Summary
Author: Mahamadou ANNE (INSA Rennes)
Supervisor: Prof. Nikos Parlavantzas
Core Objective: Extend the faas-sim discrete-event serverless edge simulator with DAG workflow orchestration, peer-to-peer direct data passing and workflow-aware scheduling policies integrated with Skippy.


Map of Content (MOC)

01 - Literature Review & Problem Statement

The shift from Cloud FaaS to the Edge-Cloud Continuum ([1] Raith et al., 2023).
The Triangular Data Transfer Trap (\text{Node}_A \to \text{Remote Storage} \to \text{Node}_B).
Insights from Skippy ([3] Rausch et al., 2021), faas-sim (Raith et al., 2023), and SONIC ([4] Mahgoub et al., USENIX ATC 2021).


02 - Architecture & Execution Lifecycle

Modular package architecture (sim/workflow/).
The 5-Step On-Time Task Execution Lifecycle in WorkflowEngine.
Integration with DefaultFaasSystem and WorkflowSkippyScheduler (env.scheduler).


03 - Data Passing Channels & Network Model

DirectDataChannel (1-hop P2P fluid flow) & automatic collapse to COLOCATED (0 network hops, RAM bandwidth).
RemoteStorageDataChannel (2-hop triangular baseline with single-upload fan-out deduplication).
Ether TCP fluid-flow physics and max-min fair bandwidth sharing.


04 - Scheduling Policies & Makespan Criteria

Pluggable WorkflowScheduler.schedule_task(...) interface.
RoundRobinWorkflowScheduler, DataAwareWorkflowScheduler, and MakespanWorkflowScheduler.
Detailed analysis of the 5 criteria of MakespanWorkflowScheduler and their relevance.


05 - Invariants, Edge Cases & Verification Suite

Self-checking architectural invariants (I-A1 through I-D).
Edge cases (E-1 through E-6) and failure/fallback handling.
Summary of the 24 automated tests in tests/test_workflow.py.


06 - Experimental Evaluation & Benchmarks

Experiment 1: 3-Stage Edge AI Pipeline (preprocess -> inference -> postprocess, 20 MB).
Experiment 2: Sensor-Anchored Payload Scaling (1 MB \to 50 MB).
Experiment 3: Parallel Video Analytics Fan-Out Scaling (K \in \{1, 2, 4, 6, 8\}).




High-Level Architecture Diagram
flowchart TB
    subgraph WorkflowLayer["sim/workflow/ Extension Layer"]
        DAG["WorkflowDAG<br/>(Tasks & DataDependencies)"]
        Sched["WorkflowScheduler<br/>(RoundRobin | DataAware | Makespan)"]
        Engine["WorkflowEngine<br/>(5-Step On-Time Orchestrator)"]
        Ctrl["DataTransferController<br/>(Direct, Colocated, RemoteStorage)"]
    end

    subgraph FaasSimCore["faas-sim Core Subsystems"]
        Faas["DefaultFaasSystem<br/>(scale_up, invoke, Replicas)"]
        Skippy["WorkflowSkippyScheduler<br/>(Extends Skippy env.scheduler)"]
        Ether["Ether Network Topology<br/>(Routes, RTT, SafeFlow)"]
    end

    DAG --> Engine
    Sched <-->|"On-time node selection"| Engine
    Engine -->|"1. Enqueue target node"| Skippy
    Engine -->|"2. Resolve/Deploy Replica"| Faas
    Faas -->|"3. Pod Predicate & Placement"| Skippy
    Engine -->|"4. Transfer Incoming Data"| Ctrl
    Ctrl -->|"Fluid-flow simulation"| Ether
    Engine -->|"5. Invoke FunctionRequest"| Faas


Quick Run Commands

.venv\Scripts\pytest.exe tests/test_workflow.py -v
 
# Run the 3 evaluation experiments and regenerate plots in examples/workflows/plots/

01---literature-review--and--problem-sta.title: 01 - Literature Review & Problem Statement
01---literature-review--and--problem-sta.content:
01 - Literature Review & Problem Statement
← Back to Index

1. The Tension Between Stateless FaaS and Data-Intensive Edge AI
Modern Edge Intelligence (EI) applications—such as urban camera video analytics, industrial IoT anomaly detection, and multi-stage ML inference pipelines—generate large volumes of intermediate data at the network edge. Offloading raw sensor streams to a centralized cloud introduces:

High and variable WAN latency over asymmetric edge uplinks (e.g., 25 Mbps cellular/uplink vs. 1 Gbps local LAN).
Backhaul bandwidth saturation when multiple edge sensors or parallel workflow branches transmit simultaneously.
Data privacy and residency constraints.

While Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) offers fine-grained autoscaling (scale-to-zero) and developer abstraction, traditional FaaS platforms treat functions as isolated, stateless invocations that exchange intermediate state via remote object storage (e.g., AWS S3 or MinIO).

2. The Bottleneck: The Triangular Data Transfer Trap
flowchart LR
    TaskA["Producer Task u<br/>(Edge Node A)"]
    Storage[("Remote Storage<br/>(Cloud / S3 / MinIO)")]
    TaskB["Consumer Task v<br/>(Edge Node B)"]

    TaskA -- "Hop 1: Upload (Slow WAN Uplink)" --> Storage
    Storage -- "Hop 2: Download (WAN Downlink)" --> TaskB
    TaskA -. "Direct Passing (1-Hop LAN / 0-Hop Colocated)" .-> TaskB

Staging ephemeral intermediate data through remote storage creates three compounding inefficiencies in heterogeneous edge-cloud topologies:

Double Network Traversal (2 Hops): Every intermediate payload traverses the network twice (\text{Producer} \to \text{Storage} and \text{Storage} \to \text{Consumer}).
Topology Blindness: Standard container schedulers (e.g., default Kubernetes scheduler) ignore link bandwidths, round-trip times (RTT), and where upstream parent tasks executed.
Missed Colocation (VM-Storage): When consecutive tasks can fit on the same node, passing data via local memory/IPC eliminates network transfer entirely (0 hops).


3. Synthesis of Reference Papers
3.1 faas-sim (Raith, Rausch, Furutanpey, Dustdar — Software: Practice and Experience, 2023)

Provides a discrete-event simulation framework built on SimPy, Ether (network topology & fluid-flow TCP modeling), and Skippy (pod scheduling).
Models realistic container lifecycles (deploy image pull from DockerRegistry, startup, setup, invoke, teardown) and heterogeneous hardware tiers (rpi3 ARM SBCs, nuc Intel i5 micro-servers, tx2 NVIDIA Jetson CUDA accelerators, and server Xeon cloudlets).
Gap in faas-sim: faas-sim only models independent single-function invocations; it has no workflow DAG abstraction, no inter-function data channels, and no workflow-aware scheduling.

3.2 Skippy ([3] Rausch, Rashed, Dustdar — FGCS, 2021)

Introduces a two-phase Kubernetes-style scheduler for single functions:

Predicates (Hard Constraints): Checks CPU, RAM, architecture (arm32, aarch64, x86), and capability labels.
Priorities (Soft Scoring): Balances image locality (10% unique container layer size vs. 90% shared base layers), storage locality, and hardware capabilities (GPU).


Insight Used in Our Work: Rather than bypassing Skippy, our WorkflowSkippyScheduler subclasses Skippy’s Scheduler (env.scheduler), preserving all Skippy predicates, image caching (images_on_nodes), and pod allocation accounting while enforcing workflow-level node placement decisions.

3.3 SONIC ([4] Mahgoub et al. — USENIX ATC, 2021)

Demonstrates that no single data-passing mode or placement strategy dominates across all workflow shapes:

VM-Storage (COLOCATED): Best for sequential chains or low fan-out when tasks fit on one host (0 network hops). However, forcing K parallel fan-out tasks onto a single host serializes execution or causes severe CPU contention.
Direct-Passing (DIRECT): Enables true parallel execution across K distinct worker nodes with a single network copy (1 hop), but shares the sender’s outgoing link bandwidth across concurrent fan-out flows:
\tau_{\text{Direct}}(S_i) = \frac{F}{\min(\text{BW}_{\text{src}} / K, \text{BW}_{\text{dst}})}
Remote-Storage (REMOTE_STORAGE): Incurs 2 serial hops on a linear chain, but in high-fan-out broadcast stages the sender uploads its output once to storage while K receivers download in parallel.

02---architecture--and--execution-lifecy.title: 02 - Architecture & Execution Lifecycle
02---architecture--and--execution-lifecy.content:
02 - Architecture & Execution Lifecycle
← Back to Index | ← Previous | Next →

1. Package Structure (sim/workflow/)
The extension is implemented as a self-contained package inside sim/workflow/ without modifying faas-sim’s core files:






























ModuleCore ClassesResponsibilitysim/workflow/model.pyWorkflowDAG, WorkflowTask, DataDependency, DataPassingModeDAG representation, duplicate/self-edge rejection, cycle detection & topological sorting via Kahn’s algorithm.sim/workflow/channel.pyDataChannel, DirectDataChannel, RemoteStorageDataChannel, ColocatedDataChannel, DataTransferControllerSimPy fluid-flow network transfers via Ether, automatic same-host COLOCATED collapse, and remote-storage fan-out upload deduplication.sim/workflow/scheduler.pyWorkflowScheduler, RoundRobinWorkflowScheduler, DataAwareWorkflowScheduler, MakespanWorkflowScheduler, WorkflowSkippySchedulerJust-in-time (on-time) task scheduling policies and Skippy cluster scheduler integration (env.scheduler).sim/workflow/engine.pyWorkflowEngine, WorkflowExecutionResult, WorkflowTaskExecutionRecordConcurrent SimPy DAG orchestration, replica resolution/deployment, data-gated invocation, and telemetry isolation.

2. The 5-Step On-Time Task Execution Lifecycle
Unlike static offline schedulers that place all tasks at t = 0 before execution starts, WorkflowEngine schedules each task just-in-time (on-time) once all of its upstream parents have completed and their actual execution nodes are known.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as Benchmark / Caller
    participant Engine as WorkflowEngine
    participant Policy as WorkflowScheduler (Policy)
    participant Faas as DefaultFaasSystem
    participant Skippy as WorkflowSkippyScheduler (env.scheduler)
    participant Channel as DataTransferController

    User->>Engine: execute_workflow(dag)
    Note over Engine: Spawn SimPy process per task.<br/>Root tasks start immediately <br/> child tasks wait on parent_done_events.

    rect rgb(235, 245, 255)
        Note over Engine,Channel: Task T Lifecycle (Executed On-Time per Task)
        Engine->>Engine: Step 1: Wait for all parent tasks of T to finish (simpy.AllOf)
        Engine->>Policy: Step 2: schedule_task(T, dag, placements, env)
        Policy->>Skippy: Probe feasible nodes via passes_predicates(probe_pod, node)
        Policy-->>Engine: Return planned_node
        Engine->>Faas: Step 3: _prepare_execution_target(T, planned_node)
        opt Cold Start (No RUNNING replica on planned_node)
            Engine->>Skippy: enqueue_placement(fn_name, planned_node)
            Engine->>Faas: scale_up(fn_name, 1)
            Faas->>Skippy: env.scheduler.schedule(pod)
            Skippy-->>Faas: Place pod on planned_node (or fallback actual_node if saturated)
            Faas->>Faas: Pull Docker image & start container -> RUNNING
        end
        Engine->>Engine: Synchronize placements[T] = actual_node<br/>Record cold_start_duration
        Engine->>Channel: Step 4: Transfer incoming payloads from placements[parent] -> actual_node
        Note over Channel: Concurrent simpy.AllOf across all incoming edges
        Channel-->>Engine: Return DataTransferRecord(s)
        Engine->>Faas: Step 5: invoke(FunctionRequest(name, replica=target_replica))
        Faas-->>Engine: Pure computation complete on actual_node
        Engine->>Engine: Record WorkflowTaskExecutionRecord (duration, cold_start_duration)<br/>Signal task_done_events[T].succeed()
    end


3. Why Replica Resolution Happens Before Data Transfer (Steps 3 \to 4)
A critical architectural design decision in WorkflowEngine._run_task is resolving or deploying the target replica in Step 3 before transferring incoming payloads in Step 4:

Saturation Fallback Correctness (Edge Case E-2): Suppose planned_node passed predicates at Step 2, but another concurrent workflow task exhausted its remaining CPU/RAM before WorkflowSkippyScheduler.schedule(pod) ran. Skippy falls back to actual_node. By resolving the replica first and updating placements[T] = actual_node, Step 4 transfers the incoming payloads to actual_node (where the replica actually runs) rather than stranding data on the rejected planned_node.
Peer-to-Peer Receiver Readiness: Direct data passing requires a running receiver container on the destination host to accept the stream.
Clean Telemetry Separation: Measuring cold_start_duration in Step 3 and duration (compute_duration) strictly around faas.invoke(request) in Step 5 prevents cold-start Docker image pulls from corrupting total_compute_time.

03---data-passing-channels--and--network.title: 03 - Data Passing Channels & Network Model
03---data-passing-channels--and--network.content:
03 - Data Passing Channels & Network Model
← Back to Index | ← Previous | Next →

1. Data Passing Modes (DataPassingMode)
DataTransferController manages intermediate data transfers across three modes (configurable globally on WorkflowDAG.default_mode or overridden per edge on DataDependency.mode):
1.1 DirectDataChannel (DataPassingMode.DIRECT)

Cross-Node (n_u \neq n_v): Executes a 1-hop peer-to-peer TCP flow directly from producer node n_u to consumer node n_v via env.flow_factory (SafeFlow / UninterruptingFlow), bypassing remote object storage (hops = 1).
Same-Host Collapse (n_u = n_v): Automatically collapses to DataPassingMode.COLOCATED with hops = 0, transferring data at host memory bandwidth (1\text{ GB/s} with a 1\,\mu\text{s} minimum syscall floor):
T_{\text{colocated}}(\text{size}) = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{size}}{10^9},\; 10^{-6}\right)

1.2 ColocatedDataChannel (DataPassingMode.COLOCATED)

Subclasses DirectDataChannel. When strict=True, raises ValueError if producer and consumer are placed on different physical hosts; otherwise executes the same zero-network-hop in-memory transfer.

1.3 RemoteStorageDataChannel (DataPassingMode.REMOTE_STORAGE)

Models the traditional cloud FaaS triangular pattern through a designated storage_node (e.g., S3 / MinIO):

Hop 1 (Upload): Producer n_u \to \text{storage\_node}.
Hop 2 (Download): \text{storage\_node} \to Consumer n_v.


Single-Upload Fan-Out Deduplication (shared_uploads): Following SONIC ([4] Section 2.1), when a producer task u fans out to K downstream consumers via REMOTE_STORAGE, the producer uploads its output to storage_node only once. Concurrent consumers await the shared upload completion event and then execute their K downloads in parallel.
Exact Network Hop Accounting:
\text{hops} = \mathbb{I}(n_u \neq n_{\text{storage}}) + \mathbb{I}(n_{\text{storage}} \neq n_v) \in \{0, 1, 2\}


2. Network Flow Physics: Paper Formulation vs. Code Implementation
In the original faas-sim paper (fass-sim.pdf, Section 3.2.7, Equations 2 & 3), the network flow duration and goodput are defined conceptually as:
\text{duration}(\text{flow}) = \text{roundtriptime} \cdot 1.5 + \left(\frac{\text{bytes to transfer}}{\text{goodput}}\right) \quad \text{[Eq. 2]}
\text{goodput}(\text{flow}) = 0.97 \cdot \min_{\text{link} \in \text{route}} \big(\text{maxAllocatablePerFlow}(\text{link})\big) \quad \text{[Eq. 3]}
While the paper expresses these relationships in abstract units (where time is implicitly in seconds and bandwidth is already in bytes per second), the actual code implementation in Ether (ether.core.Flow and ether.core.Link) incorporates physical unit conversions necessary for real network profiles and SimPy’s simulation clock:
2.1 Why Divide TCP Handshake by 1000? (/ 1000)
In ether.core.Flow.establish:
connection_time = ((route.rtt * 1.5) / 1000)  # rough estimate of TCP connection establish time

Topology Units vs. SimPy Clock: In Ether, link latencies and route RTTs are configured in milliseconds (ms) (e.g., 1\,\text{ms} LAN switch, 20\,\text{ms} WAN link).
Clock Conversion: SimPy’s event-driven clock (env.now) ticks in seconds (s).

2.2 Why Multiply Goodput by 125,000? (* 125 000)
In ether.core.Link.get_goodput_bps:
allocated = self.allocation[flow]
practical_bw = allocated * 125000
goodput_magic_number = 0.97  # rough estimate of goodput (~ TCP overhead)
return practical_bw * goodput_magic_number

Mbps to Bytes/sec Conversion: In network definitions, link capacities are expressed in Megabits per second (Mbps) (e.g., 1000\,\text{Mbps} for 1 Gbps Ethernet, 25\,\text{Mbps} for 4G/WAN uplink).
Payloads in Bytes: FaaS workflow inputs and outputs are sized in Bytes (B).
Standard conversion:
1\,\text{Mbps} = 1{,}000{,}000\,\text{bits/s}
1\,\text{Byte} = 8\,\text{bits} \implies \frac{1{,}000{,}000\,\text{bits/s}}{8\,\text{bits/Byte}} = 125{,}000\,\text{Bytes/s}
Therefore, multiplying allocated link bandwidth by 125{,}000 converts from Mbps into Bytes/s, before applying the 0.97 TCP protocol header factor (3% packet overhead).

2.3 Synthesis Formula in Simulation Units
Putting both conversions together, for a payload of S bytes across route R where \text{RTT}(R) is in milliseconds and link capacity B_e is in Mbps:
T_{\text{flow}}(n_u, n_v, S) = \underbrace{\frac{1.5 \times \text{RTT}_{ms}(R)}{1000}}_{\text{TCP Handshake (s)}} + \underbrace{\frac{S}{0.97 \times 125{,}000 \times \min_{e \in R.\text{hops}} \left(\frac{B_{e,\text{Mbps}}}{k_e}\right)}}_{\text{Data Transmission Time (s)}}
Unit Consistency Across Scheduler and SimPy
Both DataChannel (executing SafeFlow) and WorkflowScheduler._estimate_flow_time utilize this exact physical unit conversion, ensuring that the scheduler’s predictive makespan estimates match the discrete-event simulation time down to the microsecond.

04---scheduling-policies--and--makespan-.title: 04 - Scheduling Policies & Makespan Criteria
04---scheduling-policies--and--makespan-.content:
04 - Scheduling Policies & Makespan Criteria
← Back to Index | ← Previous | Next →

1. Pluggable Policy Interface (WorkflowScheduler)
All workflow scheduling policies inherit from WorkflowScheduler (sim/workflow/scheduler.py) and implement:
def schedule_task(
    self,
    task: WorkflowTask,
    workflow: WorkflowDAG,
    placements: Dict[str, str],
    env: Environment
) -> str
Three policies are implemented to represent distinct scheduling philosophies:

RoundRobinWorkflowScheduler: Baseline topology- and data-agnostic policy. Reuses idle warm replicas in round-robin order when available, and scales out across feasible nodes using a persistent counter.
DataAwareWorkflowScheduler: Pure data-locality policy (analogous to SAND / VM-Storage preference). Minimizes total incoming data transfer latency \sum_{u \in \text{parents}(v)} T_{\text{transfer}}(n_u \to n) with warm-replica preference and optional load-balancing weight.
MakespanWorkflowScheduler: Critical-path completion-time optimizer (inspired by SONIC [4] and Skippy [3]). Jointly trades off network transfer time, link contention, cold-start/image locality, hardware compute speedup, and multi-tenant node contention.


2. How DataAwareWorkflowScheduler Works
DataAwareWorkflowScheduler (sim/workflow/scheduler.py) is a data-locality-first policy (analogous to SAND’s locality preference). It filters feasible nodes via Skippy predicates (and an optional max_tasks_per_node cap using ancestor-excluded active load), then splits into two cases:
2.1 Root Tasks (\text{parents}(v) = \emptyset)
Because a root task has no incoming data dependencies, DataAwareWorkflowScheduler selects a node n \in \text{Eligible}(v) by minimizing the lexicographic tuple:
\big(\mathbb{I}(n \notin \text{Feasible}(w_{\max})),\;\; \text{ColdPenalty}(v, n),\;\; \text{ActiveLoad}(n)\big)

Downstream Co-locatability (E-1): Prefers nodes that can also host the heaviest outgoing child w_{\max} (so the subsequent edge can collapse to zero-hop COLOCATED).
Replica Warmth: Prefers nodes already hosting a warm replica of v.
Active Load: Breaks ties by lowest concurrent non-ancestor task count.

2.2 Dependent Tasks (\text{parents}(v) \neq \emptyset)
For each candidate node n \in \text{Eligible}(v), DataAwareWorkflowScheduler minimizes:
\text{Score}_{\text{DA}}(n) = w_{\text{net}} \cdot \sum_{u \in \text{parents}(v)} \hat{T}_{\text{transfer}}(n_u \to n,\; \text{size}_{u,v},\; \text{mode}_{u,v}) + w_{\text{load}} \cdot \text{ActiveLoad}(n) + \text{ColdPenalty}(v, n)
where:

Sum of Incoming Transfers (\sum): Accumulates estimated transfer time across all incoming edges (weighted by network_weight, default 1.0).
Optional Load Penalty: load_balance_weight * ActiveLoad(n) (default 0.0, i.e., pure data locality unless explicitly enabled).
Flat Cold-Start Penalty: Adds a fixed cold_start_penalty (default 0.5s) when warm replicas exist elsewhere and n \notin \text{Warm}(v) (does not model image layer pull times).
No Compute-Speed Model: Treats all hardware tiers (rpi3, nuc, tx2, server) as having identical compute speed. Consequently, for compute-heavy tasks with small payloads, it stays on a slow rpi3 to avoid a tiny transfer rather than offloading to a faster server.


3. The 5 Criteria of MakespanWorkflowScheduler
For a ready task v and each candidate node n \in \text{Feasible}(v), MakespanWorkflowScheduler minimizes:
\text{Score}(n) = T_{\text{transfer}}(v, n) + T_{\text{cold}}(v, n) + T_{\text{compute}}(v, n) + T_{\text{lookahead}}(v, n)
Criterion 1: Skippy Hardware Predicate Feasibility (\text{Feasible}(v))

Filters out switches, container registries, and storage-only nodes.
Evaluates env.scheduler.passes_predicates(probe_pod, s_node) without mutating global pod counters (_build_probe_pod), ensuring CPU, RAM, architecture (arm32, aarch64, x86), and capability labels are satisfied.

Criterion 2: Critical-Path Incoming Data Transfer & Sibling Link Contention (T_{\text{transfer}}(v, n))
T_{\text{transfer}}(v, n) = \max_{u \in \text{parents}(v)} \hat{T}_{\text{flow}}\!\left(n_u \to n,\; \text{size}_{u,v},\; k_e\right)

Uses \max_{u \in \text{parents}(v)} (rather than \sum) because incoming transfers from multiple completed parents run concurrently (simpy.AllOf).
Divides link bandwidth B_e by 1 + k_e, where k_e is the number of already-placed concurrent sibling transfers from the same parent u traversing link e (matching SONIC Equations 3–4 and Ether’s max-min fair flow allocation).

Criterion 3: Replica Warmth & Container Image Locality (T_{\text{cold}}(v, n))
T_{\text{cold}}(v, n) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n \in \text{Warm}(v) \\ \tau_{\text{base}} & \text{if } n \notin \text{Warm}(v) \text{ and image cached on } n \\ \tau_{\text{base}} + \hat{T}_{\text{flow}}(\text{Registry} \to n,\; 0.1 \times S_{\text{img}}) & \text{if image not cached on } n \end{cases}

Follows Skippy ([3] Section 4.5), where 90% of container base layers are shared across images and 10% of the image size represents unique function layers pulled from DockerRegistry.

Criterion 4: Heterogeneous Compute Speed & Active Contention (T_{\text{compute}}(v, n))
T_{\text{compute}}(v, n) = d_{\text{base}}(v) \times \frac{\text{CPU}_{\text{ref}}}{\text{CPU}_{\text{eff}}(n)} \times \big(1 + \alpha \cdot \text{ActiveLoad}(n)\big)

4-Tier Hardware Speedup (compute_node_speedup_ratio):

rpi3 (sbc, ARM Cortex-A53): 0.5\times reference speed (2{,}000\text{m} effective).
nuc (sffc, Intel Core i5): 1.0\times reference speed (4{,}000\text{m} effective).
tx2 (embai, NVIDIA Jetson TX2 CUDA): 1.5\times reference speed (6{,}000\text{m} effective).
server (Xeon 88-core cloudlet): 4.0\times single-container core cap (16{,}000\text{m} effective).


Ancestor-Excluded Contention (\text{ActiveLoad}(n)): Excludes completed ancestor tasks in the DAG (_get_ancestors) so sequential parent pods sitting idle on node n are never mistaken for active CPU contention, while counting parallel non-ancestor tasks and active in-flight requests.

Criterion 5: Root-Task Downstream Co-location Lookahead (T_{\text{lookahead}}(v, n))

When v is a root task (\text{parents}(v) = \emptyset) with a heavy outgoing edge (v \to w), if candidate node n \notin \text{Feasible}(w) (e.g., n is a 1 GB rpi3 that cannot host a 1024 MiB resnet50-inference child), adds \min_{m \in \text{Feasible}(w)} \hat{T}_{\text{transfer}}(n \to m) so the scheduler accounts for the unavoidable hop forced on child w.


Critical Assessment: Are All 5 Criteria Relevant?

Every criterion directly prevents a distinct failure mode observed in edge-cloud workflows.




































CriterionWhat Breaks If Removed?Demonstrated In1. Hardware PredicatesScheduler places 1024 MiB resnet50-inference onto a 1 GB rpi3, causing Skippy scheduling rejection or fallback.test_invariant_ie1, Experiment 1 & 22. Transfer + Sibling Link SharingWithout transfer cost, tasks scatter across WAN links (RoundRobin); without sibling link-sharing (k_e), fan-out stages send all K parallel branches over a single 25 Mbps WAN uplink to cloud servers (6.95s vs. 3.13s).Experiment 2 (1 MB \to 50 MB) & Experiment 3 (K = 1 \to 8)3. Warmth & Image LocalityConsecutive workflow arrivals ignore warm replicas and cached images, triggering unnecessary cold starts across the topology.test_full_faassim_skippy_workflow_integration, Experiment 14. Compute Speed & ContentionWithout compute speed, a compute-heavy task with a tiny 1 MB payload stays on a slow rpi3 instead of offloading to server (3.22s vs. 2.37s). Without contention (ActiveLoad), all K=8 parallel branches pile onto 1 node (7.80s vs. 3.13s).test_invariant_id, Experiment 2 (1 MB) & Experiment 3 (K = 8)5. Root Lookahead (E-1)Unpinned root task lands on rpi3 and forces a cross-node transfer for its heavy child instead of co-locating both on nuc/tx2/server with 0 network hops.test_invariant_ie1, Experiment 1

05---invariants,-edge-cases--and--verifi.title: 05 - Invariants, Edge Cases & Verification Suite
05---invariants,-edge-cases--and--verifi.content:
05 - Invariants, Edge Cases & Verification Suite
← Back to Index | ← Previous | Next →

1. Hard Architectural Invariants
All invariants are automatically verified in tests/test_workflow.py (24 passed):
Group A: DAG Integrity & Causal Ordering

I-A1 (Cycle, Self-Edge & Duplicate-Edge Rejection): WorkflowDAG.add_dependency rejects self-dependencies, duplicate (source_task, target_task) edges, and any cycle detected by Kahn’s topological sort (ValueError).
I-A2 (Strict Causal Ordering): For every dependency (u \to v):
\text{task\_records}[u].\text{end\_time} \le \text{transfer}(u \to v).\text{start\_time} \le \text{transfer}(u \to v).\text{end\_time} \le \text{task\_records}[v].\text{start\_time}
I-A3 (Parallel Branch Concurrency): Independent branches (A \to B, A \to C) transfer inputs and execute concurrently in SimPy (simpy.AllOf).

Group B: On-Time Scheduling & Skippy Integration

I-B1 (Single Policy Owner): WorkflowEngine.scheduler decides target node placement; WorkflowSkippyScheduler enforces that target node inside Skippy’s ClusterContext.
I-B2 (True On-Time Scheduling): A task v is never scheduled before all of its upstream parents \{u_i\} have completed and recorded their actual execution nodes.
I-B3 (Zero Side-Effects During Probing): The workflow scheduler is predictive and side-effect-free, probing candidate nodes via _build_probe_pod never increments sim.skippy.pod_counters or mutates cluster allocations.
I-B4 (Skippy Predicate Compliance): _get_compute_nodes excludes switches, registries, storage nodes, and nodes that fail passes_predicates.
I-B5 (Pre-Transfer Fallback Synchronization): Replica resolution happens before incoming data transfer; if Skippy falls back from a saturated planned_node to actual_node, incoming and outgoing transfers route to/from actual_node.
I-B6 (Concurrent Cold-Start Isolation): Parallel tasks targeting the same (fn, node) share a single pending deployment, while parallel tasks targeting distinct nodes (fn, node_A) and (fn, node_B) at the same timestamp claim separate replicas via _claimed_replica_ids.

Group C: Data Channels & Telemetry Isolation

I-C1 (Same-Host Colocated Collapse): DirectDataChannel automatically collapses to DataPassingMode.COLOCATED (hops = 0) when src == dst.
I-C2 (Pure Compute vs. Cold-Start Separation & Run Isolation): WorkflowTaskExecutionRecord.duration and total_compute_time measure only pure function execution time (fet), while cold_start_duration and total_cold_start_time capture cold-start provisioning.


2. Edge Cases Handled (E-1 – E-6)








































IDEdge CaseResolution & Test CoverageE-1Root Task with Constrained Downstream ConsumerDataAware and Makespan evaluate downstream child feasibility (\text{Feasible}(u) \cap \text{Feasible}(v)) so root tasks co-locate with heavy consumers (test_invariant_ie1_root_task_downstream_colocation_feasibility).E-2Target Node Saturated at Pod Scheduling TimeWorkflowSkippyScheduler falls back to Skippy priority scoring (actual_node) before incoming data transfer begins (test_invariant_ib5_fallback_actual_node_synchronization).E-3Concurrent Cold Starts on Same vs. Different NodesDeduplicated per (function_name, node_name) via _pending_waiters, _pending_replicas, and _claimed_replica_ids (test_invariant_ib6_concurrent_cold_start_isolation).E-4Completed Sequential Ancestors vs. Active Contention_get_ancestors excludes completed ancestor tasks from node load counts so sequential chains co-locate even when max_tasks_per_node=1 (test_round_robin_state_persistence_and_data_aware_ancestor_exclusion).E-5Remote Storage Broadcast Fan-OutRemoteStorageDataChannel deduplicates Hop 1 (src -> storage upload) across concurrent consumers of the same parent task via shared_uploads (test_round_robin_state_persistence_and_data_aware_ancestor_exclusion).E-6Custom Metadata in WorkflowTask.kwargs_execute_computation filters task.kwargs to valid FunctionRequest fields (size, client).

06---experimental-evaluation--and--bench.title: 06 - Experimental Evaluation & Benchmarks
06---experimental-evaluation--and--bench.content:
06 - Experimental Evaluation & Benchmarks
← Back to Index | ← Previous

1. Experimental Setup (examples/workflows/main.py)
All experiments run on faas-sim’s full discrete-event simulation engine (Simulation, DefaultFaasSystem, DockerDeploySimMixin, SafeFlowFactory) over the Urban Sensing edge-cloud topology (ether.scenarios.urbansensing), which comprises:

Edge Neighborhoods: Raspberry Pi 3 (rpi3, arm32, 1 GB RAM, 0.5\times core speed), Intel NUC (nuc, x86, 16 GB RAM, 1.0\times speed), and NVIDIA Jetson TX2 (tx2, aarch64, 8 GB RAM, CUDA GPU 1.5\times speed), connected via 500–1000 Mbps local links and a 25 Mbps shared WAN uplink to the cloud.
Cloudlet / Registry: Multi-core Xeon servers (server, x86, 88 cores, 4.0\times single-task speedup) and DockerRegistry.


2. Experiment 1: 3-Stage Edge AI Pipeline (20 MB Payload)
Workflow: preprocess (python-pi) \xrightarrow{20\text{ MB}} inference (resnet50-inference) \xrightarrow{10\text{ MB}} postprocess (postprocess-fn) (unpinned root, scale_min=0 in Run 1 Cold Start, replica reuse in Run 2 Warm Start).













































Policy & Passing ModeCold Makespan (Run 1)Warm Makespan (Run 2)Pure ComputeData TransferNode Placement (prep -> inf -> post)RoundRobin + RemoteStorage28.38s16.76s4.00s12.76srpi3_0 -> tx2_0 -> rpi3_2RoundRobin + Direct16.16s4.53s4.00s0.53srpi3_16 -> tx2_16 -> rpi3_18DataAware + Direct11.34s3.63s3.60s0.03s (COLOCATED)nuc_6 -> nuc_6 -> nuc_6Makespan + Direct1.89s0.93s0.90s0.03s (COLOCATED)server_30 -> server_30 -> server_30

Key Takeaways (Experiment 1)

Direct Passing vs. Remote Storage: Replacing REMOTE_STORAGE with DIRECT under RoundRobin cuts warm transfer latency from 12.76s to 0.53s (24x faster data movement, 3.7x lower warm makespan) by avoiding the 25 Mbps WAN uplink to remote storage.
Co-location Collapse (DataAware + Direct): Using Edge Case E-1 lookahead, DataAware places all three stages on nuc_6 (COLOCATED, 0 network hops, 0.03s RAM transfer), reducing warm makespan to 3.63s.
Critical-Path Optimization (Makespan + Direct): Makespan co-locates all three stages on server_30, combining 0.03s in-memory transfer with 4x compute speedup (0.93s warm makespan and 1.89s cold makespan).


3. Experiment 2: Sensor-Anchored Payload Scaling (1 MB \to 50 MB)
Workflow: Root task preprocess is pinned to an edge camera sensor (rpi3), and intermediate payload size scales from 1 MB to 50 MB.





















































Payload SizeRoundRobin + RemoteStorageRoundRobin + DirectDataAware + DirectMakespan + DirectMakespan Placement (prep -> inf -> post)1 MB5.73s4.84s3.22s2.37srpi3_112 -> server_74 -> server_74 (Cloudlet offload)5 MB8.22s4.94s3.30s3.30srpi3_176 -> tx2_177 -> tx2_177 (Edge GPU shift)15 MB14.44s5.20s3.47s3.47srpi3_240 -> tx2_241 -> tx2_241 (Edge GPU co-location)30 MB23.78s5.59s3.74s3.74srpi3_304 -> tx2_305 -> tx2_305 (Edge GPU co-location)50 MB36.24s6.11s4.10s4.10srpi3_368 -> tx2_369 -> tx2_369 (Edge GPU co-location)

Key Takeaways (Experiment 2)

Regime Transition (1 MB vs. \ge 5\text{ MB}): At 1 MB (compute-dominated regime), Makespan + Direct offloads inference and postprocess over the WAN to server_74 (2.37s vs. DataAware’s 3.22s). Once the payload reaches 5 MB, WAN uplink transfer delay exceeds the cloudlet compute savings, and Makespan automatically shifts placement to the local edge GPU (tx2), keeping transfer overhead below 22% at 50 MB (compared to 87% for RemoteStorage).


4. Experiment 3: Parallel Video Analytics Fan-Out Scaling (K \in \{1, 2, 4, 6, 8\})
Workflow: Directly models the SONIC ([4], Fig. 1 & Fig. 2) Video Analytics DAG: split_video (pinned to edge gateway nuc_0) scatters 2 MB video chunks to K parallel classify_i (resnet50-inference) branches, which feed 128 KB results into aggregate (postprocess-fn).





















































Fan-Out Degree (K)RoundRobin + RemoteStorageRoundRobin + DirectDataAware + Direct (Co-located on 1 host)Makespan + Direct (Distributed across accelerators)Distinct Parallel Worker Nodes (DA vs. MS)K = 15.39s4.21s3.60s2.18sDA: 1 node, MS: 1 nodeK = 25.60s4.21s4.20s2.50sDA: 1 node, MS: 2 nodesK = 45.95s4.22s5.40s2.60sDA: 1 node, MS: 4 nodesK = 65.71s3.61s6.60s2.72sDA: 1 node, MS: 6 nodesK = 85.70s4.44s7.80s3.13sDA: 1 node, MS: 8 nodes

Key Takeaways (Experiment 3)

Data Locality vs. Parallelism Trade-Off: Pure data-locality scheduling (DataAware + Direct, green curve) places all K parallel branches onto the same nuc_0 host to save the 2 MB transfer. While optimal for a single branch (K=1), it suffers severe multi-tenant CPU contention as K increases, degrading linearly to 7.80s at K=8.
Flat Fan-Out Scaling of RemoteStorage: Because RemoteStorageDataChannel deduplicates the producer’s upload (shared_uploads), RoundRobin + RemoteStorage stays nearly flat (~5.7s) across fan-out degrees K=1 \to 8, matching SONIC Fig. 6.
Link- and Contention-Aware Distribution (Makespan + Direct): By accounting for both multi-tenant node contention and sibling link-bandwidth sharing on the 25 Mbps WAN uplink, Makespan + Direct distributes the K branches across K distinct edge accelerators (tx2 GPUs + server), achieving 3.13s at K=8 (2.5x faster than DataAware + Direct).

index.title: 00 - Index & Project Overview
index.content:
Serverless Workflow & Data Passing Models in faas-sim
Project Summary
Author: Mahamadou ANNE (INSA Rennes)
Supervisor: Prof. Nikos Parlavantzas
Core Objective: Extend the faas-sim discrete-event serverless edge simulator with DAG workflow orchestration, peer-to-peer direct data passing and workflow-aware scheduling policies integrated with Skippy.


Map of Content (MOC)

01 - Literature Review & Problem Statement

The shift from Cloud FaaS to the Edge-Cloud Continuum ([1] Raith et al., 2023).
The Triangular Data Transfer Trap (\text{Node}_A \to \text{Remote Storage} \to \text{Node}_B).
Insights from Skippy ([3] Rausch et al., 2021), faas-sim (Raith et al., 2023), and SONIC ([4] Mahgoub et al., USENIX ATC 2021).


02 - Architecture & Execution Lifecycle

Modular package architecture (sim/workflow/).
The 5-Step On-Time Task Execution Lifecycle in WorkflowEngine.
Integration with DefaultFaasSystem and WorkflowSkippyScheduler (env.scheduler).


03 - Data Passing Channels & Network Model

DirectDataChannel (1-hop P2P fluid flow) & automatic collapse to COLOCATED (0 network hops, RAM bandwidth).
RemoteStorageDataChannel (2-hop triangular baseline with single-upload fan-out deduplication).
Ether TCP fluid-flow physics and max-min fair bandwidth sharing.


04 - Scheduling Policies & Makespan Criteria

Pluggable WorkflowScheduler.schedule_task(...) interface.
RoundRobinWorkflowScheduler, DataAwareWorkflowScheduler, and MakespanWorkflowScheduler.
Detailed analysis of the 5 criteria of MakespanWorkflowScheduler and their relevance.


05 - Invariants, Edge Cases & Verification Suite

Self-checking architectural invariants (I-A1 through I-D).
Edge cases (E-1 through E-6) and failure/fallback handling.
Summary of the 24 automated tests in tests/test_workflow.py.


06 - Experimental Evaluation & Benchmarks

Experiment 1: 3-Stage Edge AI Pipeline (preprocess -> inference -> postprocess, 20 MB).
Experiment 2: Sensor-Anchored Payload Scaling (1 MB \to 50 MB).
Experiment 3: Parallel Video Analytics Fan-Out Scaling (K \in \{1, 2, 4, 6, 8\}).
